title: Introduction to Public Health and Health Promotion
description: Concepts of health and disease, the history and functions of public health, determinants of health, levels of prevention, and health education and promotion.

topics.title: Concepts of Health and Disease
topics.summary: Definitions of health, disease causation models and the natural history of disease.

notes.b: The World Health Organization (1948) defined health as 'a state of complete physical, mental and social well-being and not merely the absence of disease or infirmity'. Disease is a disturbance in the structure or function of the body; illness is the person's subjective experience; sickness is the social role. Models of causation: the epidemiological triad (agent, host, environment), the web of causation (many interacting factors, useful for non-communicable diseases) and the wheel model.
k: WHO definition (1948): complete physical, mental and social well-being
Web of causation for chronic diseases

notes.b: The natural history of disease describes its course without intervention: the pre-pathogenesis phase (interaction of agent, host and environment before disease begins) and the pathogenesis phase (from infection/onset through subclinical and clinical stages to recovery, disability or death). The incubation period is the time from infection to onset of symptoms; the latent period applies to non-infectious diseases. Understanding this helps choose points for prevention.

topics.title: History and Functions of Public Health
topics.summary: Milestones in public health, the essential public health functions, and Alma-Ata.

notes.b: Public health is 'the science and art of preventing disease, prolonging life and promoting health through the organised efforts of society' (Winslow, 1920; Acheson, 1988). Milestones: Edward Jenner's smallpox vaccination (1796); John Snow's removal of the Broad Street pump handle during the London cholera outbreak (1854), founding modern epidemiology; the germ theory (Pasteur, Koch); the eradication of smallpox (declared 1980); the Alma-Ata Declaration (1978) on primary health care; the Ottawa Charter for Health Promotion (1986); the Millennium Development Goals (2000–2015) and Sustainable Development Goals (2015–2030, SDG 3 on health).
k: John Snow: cholera and Broad Street pump (1854)

notes.b: Essential public health functions include health surveillance and monitoring, outbreak investigation and control, health promotion, disease prevention (immunisation, screening), environmental health, health policy and planning, regulation and enforcement, and workforce development. In Nigeria, the Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (NCDC) leads surveillance and outbreak response; the National Primary Health Care Development Agency (NPHCDA) oversees primary health care and immunisation.
k: NPHCDA: primary health care and immunisation

topics.title: Determinants of Health and Health Inequalities
topics.summary: Social, economic, environmental and behavioural determinants of health.

notes.b: Health is shaped by determinants beyond health care: individual factors (age, sex, genetics), lifestyle behaviours (diet, physical activity, smoking, alcohol, sexual behaviour), social and community networks, living and working conditions (education, employment, housing, water and sanitation, food security, health services) and general socio-economic, cultural and environmental conditions — as shown in the Dahlgren–Whitehead 'rainbow' model. The social determinants of health are the conditions in which people are born, grow, live, work and age.
k: Social determinants: conditions where people live and work
Education and income strongly affect health

notes.b: Health inequalities are measurable differences in health between groups; health inequities are those differences that are unfair and avoidable. In Nigeria, indicators such as maternal mortality, under-five mortality and immunisation coverage vary widely by geopolitical zone, rural/urban residence, wealth quintile and mother's education. Universal health coverage (UHC) aims for everyone to receive needed services without financial hardship; Nigeria's National Health Insurance Authority (NHIA Act 2022) supports this goal. Out-of-pocket spending remains a major barrier.

topics.title: Levels of Prevention
topics.summary: Primordial, primary, secondary, tertiary and quaternary prevention with examples.

notes.b: Leavell and Clark described levels of prevention matched to the natural history of disease. Primordial prevention prevents the emergence of risk factors in a population (e.g. policies promoting healthy diets in children, tobacco-free laws). Primary prevention prevents disease in healthy people: health promotion (health education, nutrition) and specific protection (immunisation, insecticide-treated nets, condoms, iodised salt, seat belts). Secondary prevention is early detection and prompt treatment to halt progression (screening for hypertension, cervical cancer screening with VIA or Pap smear, contact tracing). Tertiary prevention limits disability and promotes rehabilitation in established disease (physiotherapy after stroke, diabetic foot care). Quaternary prevention protects patients from overmedicalisation.

Screening detects unrecognised disease in apparently healthy people. Wilson and Jungner (WHO, 1968) criteria include: the condition is an important health problem; its natural history is understood; there is a recognisable early stage; an acceptable, accurate test exists; effective treatment is available; and the cost is balanced against benefits. Examples: neonatal sickle cell screening, antenatal HIV and syphilis screening, blood pressure measurement, mammography.
k: Test must be acceptable and accurate

topics.title: Health Education and Health Promotion
topics.summary: Principles, models of behaviour change, and methods of health communication.

notes.b: Health education provides learning experiences that help people make informed health decisions. Health promotion (Ottawa Charter, 1986) is 'the process of enabling people to increase control over, and to improve, their health'. Its five action areas: build healthy public policy, create supportive environments, strengthen community action, develop personal skills, and reorient health services. Strategies: advocate, enable and mediate. Principles of health education include participation, starting from the known, credibility, motivation, reinforcement and using the local language and culture.
k: Health promotion: enabling control over health

notes.b: The Health Belief Model explains behaviour through perceived susceptibility, perceived severity, perceived benefits, perceived barriers, cues to action and self-efficacy. The Transtheoretical (Stages of Change) model (Prochaska and DiClemente) has stages: precontemplation, contemplation, preparation, action and maintenance (with possible relapse). Other models include the Theory of Planned Behaviour and the PRECEDE–PROCEED planning model. Methods include individual counselling, group talks, mass media, social media, drama, community mobilisation through traditional and religious leaders, and information–education–communication (IEC) materials in local languages.
k: Health Belief Model: susceptibility, severity, benefits, barriers
Use local languages and community leaders
